analysis.title: Bonds Aren't Cheap Yet; Goldman Says Long-End "Still Totally Bidless"
key_insights: Goldman one-delta desk head Rich Privorotsky says Treasuries are still totally bidless at the long end. PCE came in lighter but barely changed the long-end trajectory.

An October rate hike looks less likely after softer inflation data and Fed speakers, but stress remains further out the curve. Hikes have been taken out of the front end while the back end does not respond.
Long-end bond volatility expectations have decoupled from short-end anxiety. Privorotsky concludes that this really needs to calm.
Forward inflation expectations are inching higher alongside SPX and heating oil.
Payrolls (Friday) and ISM (Thursday) matter. After strong PMIs, ISM has some upside asymmetry for bonds, and a failure to confirm another acceleration could give duration some relief.
The recent rapid rise in yields has triggered several historically backed red flags, driven by the velocity of the move rather than the level.
BNP Paribas' Florian Roger identifies 5.5% on the US 10-year as the level where pressure on equities really builds. Yields are nearly there, and that is when valuations start to look excessive.

Bloomberg's Simon White argues Treasuries look cheap against stocks, GDP and the global cycle, but on their own historical terms they have more to fall before they are oversold. The 10-year has reached as high as 5.34% without drawing buyers.
The 10-year yield is more than 60 bps above the fair value implied by global central bank rate hikes, the yield curve, oil and the policy rate.
The equity risk premium (trailing earnings yield minus the 10-year yield) is negative and the lowest in over 20 years. On forward earnings it is close to the 2025 low.
Adjusted for term premium, Treasuries are less cheap but still attractive. The stock-bond price ratio is about one standard deviation rich in favor of stocks.
Versus global government bonds, Treasuries are neither undervalued nor overvalued, as US yields have risen at about the same pace as the developed-market average.

In three-quarters of prior cases where the Treasury index annual return was falling over six months and back at its mean, the return was lower three months later (50+ years of data). Treasuries are not yet oversold on this basis.

Most of the rise in nominal yields comes from real yields, with breakevens contained. White's leading indicator, based on excess liquidity, global rate hikes and the Fed policy rate, points to further real yield increases, leading by three to four months.
The US has one of the largest budget deficits among major economies and the largest primary deficit bar the UK. Interest costs are the highest in dollar terms.
Risks may become reflexive: higher yields raise volatility, which hits margining and risk limits and worsens Treasury market liquidity.
Treasuries have historically become persistently positively correlated with stocks when the 10-year stays much above 5.25% to 5.50%, reducing their value as a portfolio hedge.

The Treasury hired Jefferies' David Zervos as an adviser. Zervos said the Treasury is taking back control of the maturity of the debt. White says a government put makes the market hard to short, though not necessarily a good buy.

tension_points.bull_case: Treasuries look cheap versus nominal GDP and bund yields, versus stocks (negative equity risk premium, lowest in over 20 years), and the 10-year is over 60 bps above model fair value.
tension_points.bear_case: Treasuries are not yet oversold on their own history, real yields are set to keep rising, deficits are large, and rising volatility could worsen liquidity. Buyers have not emerged despite the cheapness.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 10-year yield above 5.5%, where BNP says equity pressure builds and Treasuries turn positively correlated with stocks, would undercut the hedge case for buying.
